Subject: Interlocking H&S
This is called an interlocking H&S whereby the right shoulder of the head of the topping pattern becomes the left shoulder of the inverted H&S. This can be a powerful pattern. The target is determined by projecting the measurement of the H&S top upwards from the top of the left shoulder of the inverted structure.

Below we see the front contract for crude oil, as well as its 9-month forward (purple line). For WTI the spread is $109 vs $75. That’s called backwardation, and the lazy interpretation (of which I have been guilty) is that the oil market believes that the current supply squeeze is temporary and that “this too shall pass.” In other words, $75 is the true price for oil and $109 is just a transitory glitch. I have always thought of the oil strip like the SOFR curve, paying less attention to what’s happening now and caring more about what the market is pricing in for the future. But perhaps that downward sloping strip is creating a false sense of complacency. From what I have learned, the forward curve is very illiquid and less likely to represent a collective view about future oil prices and more likely to be just the mathematical expression of the “convenience yield.” The convenience yield is the sum of the cost of carry (funding plus storage plus insurance) and the scarcity premium (or discount). The bottom panel below shows that the crude oil market has never been more stressed than it is currently, with a scarcity premium of around 60%.

Not to rain on this bullish parade, but there is a left tail lurking out there in the Strait of Hormuz. The more I learn about the mechanics of the energy market, the more concerned I am that what the market thinks is a temporary shock may well have longer term and far-reaching repercussions.

Below we see two oil analogs. The orange analog is the short-lived 1990 Gulf War. It was over as soon as it started, and oil prices retraced all their gains while stocks retraced all their losses. The purple analog is the post-COVID oil spike in 2022. That one lasted longer and produced a larger and longer lasting correction. Clearly the markets are betting on (or hoping for) the former, but I fear that with every passing week it may become the latter.

This is absolutely insane:

Alphabet, $GOOGL, Nvidia, $NVDA, Amazon, $AMZN, Broadcom, $AVGO, and Apple, $AAPL, have collectively accounted for ~50% of the S&P 500's total gains since April 1st.

This means these 5 stocks have added ~6 percentage points to the +12% rally of the index over this period.

Alphabet led the group, adding ~2 percentage points to index growth, with a +38% gain.

This was followed by Nvidia at ~1.5 points with a +21% return, Amazon at ~1 point with a +30% gain, and Broadcom at ~0.8 points with a +33% surge.

Apple contributed ~0.7 points, rising +13% over the same period.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 equal-weighted index, a gauge of the average stock performance, has increased by just +6% since the beginning of April.

Big tech is carrying the market at a historic pace.

As remarkable as these data points are, we must remember that this is a top-heavy market with top-heavy earnings. So, there is less than meets the eye here as the broader market is producing more typical earnings breadth. Nevertheless, this is the AI capex boom in action, as the next chart illustrates. Since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022, capex as a percentage of revenues has doubled to 9%, while revenues themselves have also grown.

This huge quarterly jump has lifted the calendar year 2026 growth rate to 22%. Since earnings bottomed in 2023, the growth rates have been +11% in 2024, +13% in 2025, and now +22% in 2026. https://t.co/w67HBBrIMW

Q1 earnings seasons continued last week, and the results were dramatic. I have been tracking the Bloomberg weekly estimates for over a decade, transcribing the growth rates by hand every weekend. The pattern is familiar: estimates tend to drift lower as we approach earnings season, and then lo and behold companies beat estimates by 300 bps on average. As you can see below, that has not been the pattern over the past year or so. Estimates have been drifting higher instead of lower and the bounces have been stronger than usual. And then there was last week. Wow. The growth estimate started earnings season at 14% and has exploded to 26%. Outside of recoveries from recessions (see Q1 2021 below), this just doesn’t happen.

Here's another look. The dollar estimates for Q1 came into the quarter at $71/share and has now jumped $9 to $80/share. That bounce is about three times the norm (and earnings season isn’t over yet).

All those corrections were sharp but short-lived, as is typical during secular bull markets. By my count, the current secular regime started in 2009 and is now 17 years old. There are no signs yet that the secular bull is losing its mojo. If anything, the current AI-driven capex boom is adding more muscle to this aging bull, as the chart below shows. The S&P 500 index is not only moving further above the 150-year central trendline (pink), but even the secular trendline (yellow).

The cyclical bull market started 42 months ago on October 13, 2022. It has weathered several squalls, including October 2023 when the 10-year yield reached the red line of 5.0%, the summer of 2024 when the unwinding of the yen carry trade caused a short-lived 10% drawdown, the spring of 2025 when the tariff tantrum caused a 21% drop, and most recently the Iran conflict, which so far has produced a 10% drawdown.

My sense has been that the market is interpreting the backwardated oil strip as a glass half full, concluding that the forward price of $75 is “right” and that the spot price of $109 is temporary.  But what if it’s the other way around?  What if the front contract is right and the forwards are too low?  What if the strip doesn’t tell us much about the market’s view, and instead is just telling us that the energy markets are in a state of acute stress?  What if this stress lasts longer than the market is expecting or hoping?  If so, with correlations trending as they are, it could spill over to all asset classes (equities, bonds, commodities, etc.), not to mention the economy at large, with implications for both monetary and fiscal policy.  A tale of two tails indeed.
